name: Chaos Corona
tagline: Photorealistic CPU/GPU renderer plugged into 3ds Max and Cinema 4D.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: A coding agent can absolutely write you a path tracer in an afternoon, and it will produce a pretty sphere on a checkerboard. Corona is a production renderer: adaptive sampling, caustics, a physically based material library, an AI denoiser, volumetrics, hair, displacement, and interactive render that updates while an artist drags a light. On top of that it lives inside 3ds Max and Cinema 4D as a plugin, reading their scene graphs, modifiers, instancing, and animation, which is years of host integration work no one one-shots. Even if you matched the math, you would not match the minutes-per-frame, and render time is the whole product. The consolation build is a real path tracer that teaches you exactly why this costs money.
coreLoopDIY: Loads a glTF scene plus an HDRI, traces it with a brute force progressive path tracer on the CPU, and writes a denoised PNG.
requirements: a glTF or OBJ test scene
a lot of CPU time and patience
whatYouLose: Any plugin integration with 3ds Max or Cinema 4D, so no real scenes, modifiers, or instancing
Interactive render that reacts to viewport edits in near real time
Adaptive sampling, light solvers, and caustics, which is the difference between 4 minutes and 4 hours
The material and asset libraries artists actually build with
Production features: motion blur, hair, volumetrics, displacement, render elements, distributed rendering
moatNotes: The performance work is the product. Sampling strategy and denoising are where a decade of engineering hides, and they are invisible until you try to reimplement them.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because studios bill by the hour and renders block deliveries. A renderer that converges twice as fast on a 400GB archviz scene pays for itself in a week, and it has to do that from inside the DCC the artist already models in, with the materials the rest of the team shares. Nobody is swapping that out for a hobby tracer that reads glTF.
notes: A toy path tracer is a weekend; a production renderer is a decade. The moat is twenty years of sampling and denoising research welded into 3ds Max and Cinema 4D, where the artists already live.
prompt:
Build a standalone offline path tracer in Rust. Empty folder, cargo project, CLI only.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Rust stable, no GPU, no wgpu, CPU only.
- rayon for parallelism, image for PNG output, gltf for scene loading, glam for math.
- Single binary: `cargo run --release -- scene.gltf --hdri env.hdr --spp 512 --out render.png`.

In scope:
- Load a glTF 2.0 file: meshes, transforms, node hierarchy, camera (use the first camera, fall back to a default if absent).
- Build a BVH over triangles with a surface area heuristic split. This matters more than anything else for speed, do it properly.
- Unidirectional path tracer with Russian roulette termination after depth 4, hard cap at depth 16.
- Materials: a single principled-ish BSDF with base color, roughness, metallic, and emissive, read from glTF PBR metallic-roughness. Cosine-weighted diffuse plus GGX specular with importance sampling. No clearcoat, no sheen, no subsurface.
- Lighting: emissive triangles plus an equirectangular HDR environment map. Importance sample the environment with a 2D CDF, do not just uniformly sample the sphere.
- Next event estimation to the environment and to emissive triangles, with multiple importance sampling between BSDF and light sampling.
- Progressive rendering: write the PNG every 32 samples per pixel so the user can watch it converge and kill it early.
- Tone map with ACES approximation, then sRGB encode on output. Keep the internal framebuffer linear f32.
- Deterministic per-pixel RNG seeded from pixel index plus sample index so renders are reproducible.

Out of scope, do not build:
- Any GUI, viewport, or web server.
- Motion blur, depth of field beyond a simple aperture flag, volumetrics, hair, displacement, subsurface scattering.
- A denoiser. Instead, print a note in the README that production renderers lean on OIDN or OptiX and that brute force convergence is why this is slow.
- Accounts, telemetry, network calls of any kind.

Deliverables:
- src/ split into bvh.rs, camera.rs, material.rs, sampling.rs, scene.rs, main.rs.
- A README with the exact command to render the bundled test scene and a table of spp versus wall clock on a 8-core machine.
- No secrets needed, so no .env. If you add one, you have misunderstood the task.
